text: The orchestra was playing the Romanian “Doina.” More precisely, only Ancheto was playing, with a flute solo, while the others accompanied her. We were listening from the inner salon. But, you may ask, who are these “we”? Who indeed? It is well known who: the Senator, Othello, Stuvencho, and I. In front of us stood a long bottle of white Chateau Sandrovo and another of Giesshuebler. Carefree, seated around the table with cigarettes in our mouths, we caught the fiorituras of “Doina” and had surrendered ourselves to pleasant *far niente*. Tomorrow is Sunday—there’s no work, so we can stay a little later. The music is decent, the girls are pretty, and we—somewhat overripe bachelors. Perfect!

We were sitting like that when, all of a sudden, the flute irritated my ear with a few false notes, and at the same time the whole orchestra went out of tune. In that very moment Stuvencho burst out laughing and cried: “That damned Othello! What a terrible wag! Just look at him!...” The two of us, the Senator and I, turned around at once, and what did we see! Damn Othello! Where does he get such tricks from? He had stood up without our noticing, asked for a piece of lemon, and, having beckoned the flutist over with certain signs, without the others noticing, began to tease her, to make her mouth water with the lemon juice. Well, bless you, she was a young girl, she had a craving for something sour, her mouth filled with saliva, her lips puckered—go on after that and play the flute! Laughter...

The music stopped. From the street came the shout of a boy: “No-vi-ne-spa-per-s! People’s greatness!” What People’s greatness? As if! Infected with laughter from the lemon comedy, we burst out laughing again. At that moment, here came Gedros rushing up as well.
— Oh, Gedros, hi! Sit down! Would you like some wine?
— Oh, Othello, hi, hi, little chick. Go wipe your little nose — cooed the eternally cheerful Gedros.
— Gedros, what is this newspaper, they were shouting from the street just now?
— What! Don’t you know about Bay Ganyo Balkanski’s newspaper?
— Wisecracker!
— I’m serious. Ganyo Balkanski, editor-owner of the newspaper “Narodno Velichie.” Ah, it’s quite a story. Don’t you know?
— Are you serious?
— Seriously, bro. Wait till I tell you. Today they told me this story in detail, and I’ll pass it on to you just as if I had been there.
We ordered the door of the inner room to be closed, and Gedros began. Here is what he told us:

At Bay Ganyo’s, a meeting had been called. Those gathered were: the host himself, Gochoolu, Dochoolu, and Danko the Rascal, and they were considering what sort of enterprise to take up in order to make the most advantageous use of the situation.

— We, too, ought to peck at something — says Bay Ganyo — patriotism on an empty stomach like that — boshlaff. Now tell me, as things stand, where can the best profit be made? You, Gochoolu, what do you say?
— Me? To tell you the truth, Bay Ganyo, I still stick to my own idea: let’s open a Russian tavern.
— What?!
— Let’s open a Russian tavern — Gochoolu replies seriously and decisively.
— Well, you — how? Did you get mixed up with the Matushka again? — wonders Bay Ganyo.
— But come, let’s sort this out; it’s not about Mother Russia here, the point is — what wind is blowing...
— Where? In your head?

— In Bulgaria. A fool is the one who does not take advantage. Now is the time — a tavern. I have been around Muscovy; I understand a thing or two. A tavern with two sections — one for the nobility and one for the peasants.
— Where on earth would you find men like that among us! — asks Bay Ganyo in bewilderment.
— Well then, are we all nobles at last, eh, Bay Ganyo?
— Good, what next?
— Further on: we’ll strike up some music for him, an organ—you must have seen one, Bay Ganyo?
— If I don’t see it, who will? — replies Mr. Balkanski haughtily.

— You’re right. One organ and, of course, tea. We’ll buy a dozen kids, but not dark-eyed ones, so they look like little Russians; we’ll shove a pair of boots on them, a red shirt, and then we’ll give them a Cossack haircut — there you have a whole tavern! We’ll bring in Russian newspapers, vodka snacks, and then put up a sign on top — “Russian Tavern,” — and tilt your hat to one side. Eh?
— I do not approve! — cried Dochoolu solemnly. — I do not approve! If the matter is to make a profit from the wind that has blown, then the best thing will be to open a factory for kvass...
— We hit the jackpot! — laughed Danko the Rogue. — Do you want to open a bakery?
— No, brother — I mean Russian kvass. It’s one of those things... like that, call it pear drink, call it boza...
— Nice work! So now we’re going to become boza sellers — Harsazina says offended.

— No, kardeş, it’s not about the drink — the name is what matters; let’s just say: “Russian kvass”! — they’ll kill themselves running. Haven’t you heard what the French are doing now? They’ve struck gold, gold — no joke!
— Nonsense. I don’t want yeast — said Danko, displeased.
— Well, what do you want? — Dochoolu asks him angrily. — Go on, tell us, let’s see?
— Let’s found a bank! — blurts out Danko the Scoundrel.
— You are a fool!
— Why?
— Leave the quarrels aside — Bay Ganyo interjects.
— Why should I be a fool! — Dancho continued angrily and shot murderous glances at Dochoolu.
— Well, be quiet now, sit down. Tell me, what do you have to say about the bank.
— But let him say it, my dear, why should I be a fool?
— A bank is going to found me! This thing isn’t popara to slurp up — growls Dochoolu under his mustache, unsettled by Danka’s looks and threatening tone. — Is this a popara — a bank!
— Popara is a grain! — roars the Harsuzina.
— How come “popara”? Why on earth would it be “popara”? — Dochoolu bared his teeth.
— Be quiet, people. Is that why we’ve gathered here? — Bay Ganyo calms them down. — Dochoolu, sit down in your place.
— But why on earth should it be a popara?

Word for word, the matter had come to a head; Danko the scoundrel, as you know him, goes in for a fight, and Dochoolu is no slouch either — they’ll kill each other, especially with Bay Ganyo on this side and that — he calmed them down.

Danko sits down in his place and begins to lay out his plan for founding a bank. “The job is easy — we’ll issue five to ten million in shares, pocket the money, lend to this one, lend to that one, of course at a good interest rate, to merchants, to municipalities, and if the government happens to be in a tight spot — a million or two for it as well. Well! Let’s say they draw up some bylaws, half the profit for us, half for the shareholders. Besides — we’ll keep some shares for ourselves, whether we invest money or not. You, Bay Ganyo, are an influential man, you’ll clear your throat at two or three kapias and that’s the end of it!”
— This job is not a spoon for your mouth; there are more capable people than you, let them hatch it out, and then we’ll poke our beaks in — says Bay Ganyo in a patronizing tone.
Gochoolu and Dochoolu nod their heads approvingly.

— Wait, let me tell you now what I’ve got in mind — cries out Bay Ganyo authoritatively and stands up. — Do you know with what? Neither with an inn shall we get anywhere, nor shall we set up a proper bank, and as for your Russian kvass, Dochoolu, that’s downright a simple matter; but shall I tell you what?
Gochoolu, Dochoolu, and Harsuzina are turned into rumor and impatience.
— Shall I tell you what? Huh?
— Well, say it then, stop keeping silent — Danko says nervously.
— Shh! The quick bitch gives birth to blind ones. Shall I tell you? Huh? Gentlemen! Let’s publish a newspaper! — blurts out Bay Ganyo, and triumph lights up his face.

If some sea monster had slipped into the room of our interlocutors at that moment, it could hardly have heightened the overwhelming impression produced by Bay Ganyo’s last words. In the first minute they stood as if petrified; in the next, Gochoolu, Dochoolu, and Danko Harsazina began to glance at one another timidly, as if asking: “Could it be that, God forbid, some screw has flown out of Bay Ganyo’s head?” One feels neither like laughing nor like pitying him. He’ll boil over. At last Gochoolu, fear or no fear, decides to hint at it to him from afar:
— Your grace, Bay Ganyo, you sometimes, he-he, pardon me, I mean, you like... this-and-that... practical jokes, so my point is, he-he...
— What?
— No, Bay Ganyo, I only said that just to... you know... Well, your grace, something about a newspaper... seriously?

— What do you mean, “seriously”? Why, how else? Of course seriously! Is it such a big trick to publish a newspaper? Put a blindfold over your eyes (though there’s no need), and then curse left and right. Why, of course!
— Well, if that’s the case, I agree — says Danko Harsuzina.

— Of course, how else! We’ll call Gunya Advokatina; he’s a master of leading articles, and we—some news items, some brief notices, some telegrams. If the job is to smear this one or that one, that doesn’t require any great philosophy. Danko, do run over, please, to the editorial office and call Gunya Advokatina here.

— Do you see that haiduk? — said Bay Ganyo after Danko Harsuzina had gone out. — If it comes to cursing, leave him be! He’ll curse you so that your kidney will sting. He’ll make a mati-mascar of a man. But whether right or wrong, his eye doesn’t even blink. A terrible vagabond!

Gochoolu and Dochoolu could not be said to have been delighted by these qualities of Danka Harsuzina; nor could it be said that, in their conception of journalism, Danko appeared to be a suitable editor. They still preserved memories of another time and of Turkish times, when the printed word did, after all, muddy their waters, but did not erupt into that lava of infernal abuse and curses. But the storm of wild passions, raging over the course of a whole series of years, but the demoralizing influence of the demoralized press, but the crude all-devouring materialism, but the possibility of easy enrichment through a lullabying of conscience after the example of the ruling elements — all these phenomena have covered their purer feelings with such a thick layer that it will take an entire epoch, no less long-lived and new in its essence, to dig away this layer of abominations, until those buried pure feelings emerge as remnants of former greatness.

And now, when Bay Ganyo lays out his plan for publishing a newspaper, for its direction, and for the people who will take part in it—Gochoolu and Dochoolu feel that something is stinging them in some remote corner of their hearts; they sense that there is something crooked in this business, something that ought not to be. But upon the heavy layer that presses these pure feelings down to the bottom, Bay Ganyo adds a new layer and suffocates them. With sweet eloquence, with enthusiasm, with passion, he sets forth the material advantages that will be gained from their enterprise. And for Gochoolu and Dochoolu, no more convincing arguments are needed.
The door opens and at the threshold appears Gunyo Advokatina with his fox-like sharp muzzle, followed by Danko Harsuzina entering after him.
— Ganyo, what do you say? — turns to him in a friendly way Bay Ganyo. — We want to publish a newspaper, eh?
— Why not, let’s publish it. Is there anything to be blind about? — Ganyo asks with a wink and a quick twitching of his fingers.
— You just enjoy yourself.
— But is there?
— There is, there is, enjoy yourself.
— Good. What newspaper are we to publish — for the government or for the opposition? Say quickly, because clients are waiting for me.
— That’s the catch there now — whether government or opposition? I don’t know, damn it, how long today’s lot will last.
— Say it quickly, because clients are waiting for me.
— You know what, Gunyo? — Bay Ganyo reasoned, without paying any attention to the lawyer’s words. — I think for now we should keep going with the government...
— So, so, best with the government — Gochoolu and Dochoolu hurry to declare.

Bay Ganyo looks at them angrily for cutting him off, and continues:

— ...And then, once we sniff out that their legs are starting to wobble, give them a good kick and get the new ones back in power, eh?
— Fine. Did they promise you anything?
— Of course, without it, it can’t be done.

— Since that is so, let’s begin — decides Gunyo Advokatina, and here they get into a discussion about the way they will publish the newspaper, and about a certain kind of direction their organ will follow on particular issues. It is decided that they will adapt to the times and circumstances, and to profit too, if “God has so willed it.” For Russia, “we shall print one line: our liberator, the brotherly Russian people, long live the Tsar Liberator (may God rest his soul), but otherwise, if things get rough, we’ll go back to our old ‘Danubian province.’ For Macedonia we’ll keep quiet, you know, somehow it doesn’t fit, the times are not favorable. Austria, this and that, the Triple Alliance — it doesn’t suit us at all...”
— Well, what are we going to do about the young men, about the young men? — Gochoolu chimes in. — They’ve started to stir about too!
— We’ll fool them, what can you do, foolish kids, sometimes you’ll even have to tip your hat to them, such times have come, there’s nothing to be done — said Bay Ganyo with a sigh.
— Is there nothing to be done?! — growls Danko the Rascal, and his eyes darken. — Damn unpruned stick! If I get my hands on them, then...
— Stand still, Danko...
— P... p-p-rrash and ash...
— Leave them now, don’t! Sit back in your place. There’s time.
— Come on, quicker, Bay Ganyo, clients are waiting for me — Gunyo the Lawyer calls impatiently.

— Listen, Gunyo, do you know... (hey, leave off with your damned clients!)... do you know what? You sit down tonight and write an editorial. Give it a good dose of loyal submission, so that even the prince himself will be astonished. Put in there: Your humble children, Our father and daddy, in the dust of Your August feet, arrange them there like a rosary, you know how. Then mention the people too, with one or two words, as is proper. Do you understand me? Good. Then give the opposition a good coating of tin. Say there: Those traitors, those...
— “Traitors” is old-fashioned now; let’s put “scoundrels” — Ganyo corrects.

— Well then, put in “scoundrels.” And don’t forget to put in “fatal for the Bulgarian people” as well. Damn it, I really like that word “fatal”! When I say it like that, fff... f... fatal, it’s as if I’m grabbing someone by the throat... I like it terribly!
— And as for me, I like it best when I give someone a good cursing — Danko Harsuzina blurted out candidly — it lightens my soul, I don’t know how!

— Bravo, be, Harsuz, long live you! — exclaims the delighted Bay Ganyo and pats Danka on the shoulder. — The matter is settled. You, Gunyo, will write, as I said, the leading article, right? And you, Gochoolu, and you, Dochoolu, some dispatches, some telegrams to whip up.
— What telegrams, what dispatches? — the two ask in bewilderment.

— What kind? Any kind. Don’t you see the other newspapers? Write there: Your Royal Highness, the people rejoice on their knees and unanimously beseech the Almighty... and so on; stuff in there whatever comes to mind. Say there: The Bulgarian people have given thousands of proofs that when their rights are touched, all of them rise to their feet... and... that sort of thing... with tears in their eyes... and so forth. At last, why should you scribble so much? Curse the opposition, and that’s that. Well! Why should we now sit around getting sentimental with all sorts of philosophies. And who’s going to understand you! The point is to throw dust in people’s eyes — drive on. Isn’t that so?
— Well, goodbye then, I’ve got clients waiting for me — muttered Gunyo the Lawyer, and took his hat.
— The devils are waiting for you... Well then. Come on, goodbye. And listen, Ganyo, have the introductory piece ready early tomorrow. Best regards!
Gunyo heads toward the door. After him, Gochoolu and Dochoolu stand up, to whom Bay Ganyo gives the necessary instructions.
— Listen, gentlemen, we’ve forgotten the most important thing — cried Bay Ganyo after them — but how are we going to name our newspaper?
— All right, then, Bay Ganyo, but we are... such people! — Gochoolu and Dochoolu respond.

— This is a serious matter — says Gunyo the Lawyer — and do you know why it is serious? Because those devils took all the good names and left none for us. But one can still be found. I think the most fitting thing is to name our newspaper “Justice,” and then add in parentheses a fine du siècle. (ed. note — the end of the century, Fr.)
— What?
— It is a French word; you do not understand it.
— We don’t want French; Latin, if you can, put in something, just for form’s sake.
— Shall we give it a “Tempora mutantur”?...
— Pull it if it’s in place. And you, Gochoolu, what’s your opinion? — Bay Ganyo turns to him.
— “Justice” is a nice word, but it seems to me that “Folk Wisdom” would be even nicer — replies Gochoolu.
— I don’t agree — Dochoolu calls out, — that name looks too priestly; it would be better to call it “Bulgarian Pride.”
— Well then, you, Harsuz, what do you say?
— Me? How should I know? Let’s slap on a “People’s Bravery,” and let whatever happens, happen. We’ll put Sarı-Çizmeli Mehmeda as the responsible editor, eh?
— It’s all boshlaff. Shall I tell you? — says Bay Ganyo authoritatively. — We’ll name our newspaper either “Bulgaria for Us” or “National Grandeur.” Choose one of the two.
— “People’s Grandeur”! Agreed! “People’s Grandeur”! So, so, long live!
— Farewell, Bay Ganyo.
— Goodbye.
Gochoolu, Dochoolu, and Gunyo the Lawyer come out.
— You, Danko, stay; you and I will write short editorial pieces.

— Good. Order them now to bring mastika and appetizers, and let’s get to work. And make sure they don’t drag in sour okra again; see to it that they bring some proper appetizer there — there’s a newspaper to be written here, this is no joke.
They brought mastika and meze. But Uncle Manolcho will ask, what meze? That’s not important; what matters is that Bay Ganyo and Danko the Rogue rolled up their sleeves to guide public opinion.
— Danko, our neighbor is really showing off to me, he says he’s educated, honest, and all sorts of nonsense. Shall we give him a good beating?
— Not with tin, but with the earth itself we’ll make it — declares the specialist in curses.

And then the writing begins... “We learn that...” — writes Bay Ganyo and sets down on a sheet of white paper such black slanders against his neighbor as not only has he never “learned” at any time, but which have never even crossed his mind in a dream.

Bai Ganyo writes, writes and crosses out, he is always dissatisfied with the venomousness of his arrows: thief is too gentle a word for him, he crosses it out and writes bandit, but that word has become commonplace, Bai Ganyo adds midday and combines it with a fatal one. The neighbor, his wife, his children, his kin — under Bai Ganyo’s pen they come out as phenomenal monsters... He reads his work to Danka Harsazina. Danko, with eyes shining from the mastika, enthusiastically encourages the master of the short squibs.
— Drive, drive, drive! Ram it, damn it, don’t stop at anything, at anything! Ram it! — Danko Harsuzina thunders, as if he were commanding some artillery battle...
— Here, gentlemen, is how Bay Ganyo’s organ was established — Gedros concludes his story.
We opened the door to the inner salon again, and the orchestra burst into the wonderful march from Wagner’s *Tannhäuser*.
Forgive me, indulgent reader! You will encounter in this little book some cynical words and scenes; I could not avoid them. If you can portray Bay Ganyo without cynicism—please, be my guest!

Forgive me too, Bay Ganyo! God is my witness that I have always been inspired by good feelings in describing your stories. Neither a feeling of malicious censure, nor contempt, nor frivolous laughter has guided my pen. I too am a child of my time, and certain separate events may perhaps have involuntarily diverted me from strict objectivity, but I strove to reproduce the essence of the sad reality. Your brothers, I believe, are not such as you are portrayed, Bay Ganyo, but for now they are in the second and third plan; they are only just beginning to declare their existence, whereas you—you are here, your spirit flies and envelops the whole social order and leaves its imprint on politics, on parties, and on the press. I nurture within myself the faith that a day will come when you, after reading this little book, will pause to think, will sigh, and will say: We are Europeans, but still not quite!...
Farewell, it is not a wonder for us to meet again.
Sofia, 17 March 1895.
